sentences.text: The onus to prove this issue was on the workman.
Workman in order to prove this issue has relied upon evidence of WW-1 Sh. Makan Singh, who happens to be the General Secretary of the Union.

Further Ex. WW1/2 are placed on record which are the minutes of meeting/espousal wherein names of President, Vice President, General Secretary, Treasurer etc. have been mentioned and their signatures have been appended in front of their names which have been signed and supported by workmen.

Workmen also examined Sh Anand S/o Late Sh. Jasod Singh as WW-3 who also ID No. 9271/16 Page No. 12 of 32  supported the claim of the workmen and reiterated the facts as mentioned in the statement of claim.

Workmen in their evidence relied upon documents Ex. WW1/M1 and Ex. WW1/M2 is the original register containing the minutes of meeting dated 10.06.2016 and Ex. MW1/3 is containing various documents i.e.
Memorandum of Settlement, annual return of the union and the letters addressed by the office bearers of the union to the management regarding their demands.

16. Ld. AR for the management has argued that the present dispute is not properly espoused by the union as WW-1 in his cross-examination replied to a question put by ld. AR for the management that "Q- Was any legal authority given to you by the workmen in order to file their case in this Tribunal?

A: No.",
However, this tribunal cannot lose site of the fact that the workmen has himself placed on record the minutes of the meeting dated 10.06.2016 held by the Union, which is a registered Union,
wherein the workmen have authorised the General Secretary i.e.
Maha Sachiv to take up the cause of the workman so as to raise an Industrial Dispute in their favour.
Even otherwise, the technicalities should not come in the way of dispensation of justice.

17. The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Omji Srivastava and Ors. vs. P.W.D./C.P.W.D., 2023/DHC/002013,
wherein the Hon'ble Delhi High Court after relying upon the case of Hon'ble Supreme Court in J.H. Jadhav v. M/s Forbes Gokak Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 1089 of 2005, decided on 11.02.2005 has held that the cause of the workman is properly espoused by the union.

The relevant portion of the judgment is reproduced below:
ID No. 9271/16 Page No. 15 of 32  "Learned counsel for the respondent fairly cannot  dispute the position that the view taken by the  Labour Court on the issue of espousal of the  petitioners cause is hyper technical.
There is no  dispute about the fact that the union had held its  meeting on 22.10.2005 and decided to espouse the  petitioners cause, on which date, the espousal letter  was also issued by the union.

Merely because Sh.
 B.K. Prasad may not have been the president of the  union on the said date and he became the president  in the year 2007, would make no difference.
Such a  hyper technical view defeats the objective of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
The mere wrong  description of the designation of Sh. B.K. Prasad in  the espousal letter would not render the fact of  espousal of the petitioners cause unreliable.
Pertinently, the MCD General Mazdoor Union is a  recognized union and the said union has not come  forward to claim that they had not espoused the  cause of the petitioners on 22.10.2005.

Accordingly,
 the decision of the Labour Court on issue no.2 is  reversed.
It is held that the petitioners cause was  duly espoused by the MCD General Mazdoor  Union."
20. In view of the judgments cited above, it is amply clear that there is no procedure prescribed for espousal but it depends upon the facts and circumstances of the same.

In view of the above discussion, mandate of law coupled with the aforementioned documents relied upon by the workmen have amply proved on the record that the cause of the workmen has been properly espoused by the Union i.e. Chelmsford Club Ltd Karamchari Union.

Issue no.2:
 Terms of reference.

"1. Whether the workmen are entitled to  20% increment on gross salary who have  completed 21 years of service, 15%
 increment on gross salary, who have  completed 11 to 20 years of service, 10%

21.

The workmen have demanded that they are entitled to 20% increment on gross salary who have completed 21 years of service, 15% increment on gross salary who have completed 11 to 20 years of service, 10% increment on gross salary who have completed 1 to 10 years of service with the management.
It is an undisputed fact that the workmen, regardless of their years of service, receive the same minimum wages as fixed and revised by the appropriate government.

However, this Tribunal recognizes that ID No. 9271/16 Page No. 17 of 32  the determination of wages cannot be limited solely to the statutory minimum, as it fails to account for the invaluable contributions and expertise provided by the workmen over the years.

Meaning thereby, both the categories of workmen who have recently joined the employment of the management and those who have been dedicatedly working for the management for as long as 25 years or more get equal wages.
22. The Chelmsford Club, being a well known establishment in the posh localities of Lutyens Delhi, owes much of its reputation and success to the dedication and hard work of its workmen.
These workmen have spent a significant portion of their lives in service to the management, displaying practical skills and experiences vital to the club's daily operations.
Their hands-on expertise, spanning various domains such as maintenance and customer service, forms the very backbone of the club's functionality.
The Tribunal recognizes that the loyalty and dedication exhibited by the workmen towards the Chelmsford Club have been instrumental in ensuring stability and continuity in management.

Their unwavering Chelmsford Club Limited Karamchari ... vs . on 3 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/159780183/
12 commitment to the club's ethics and values has fostered trust and a positive reputation to the management.

sentences.text: The workmen's sense of purpose and willingness to go the extra mile have contributed to the club's success in manifold ways, from upholding high service standards to adapting to dynamic needs and challenges.

Moreover,
the workmen's deep understanding of the operations of club,
culture, and clientele showcases their professionalism and competence.

Therefore, it is evident that the role of the workmen in the success/smooth functioning of the club is not ancillary but centralyl, making them the driving force behind the reputation of ID No. 9271/16 Page No. 18 of 32  the club for excellence.

23. This Tribunal firmly believes that recognizing and rewarding the contribution of the workmen through an annual increment is not just a matter of fairness but a reflection of the value they bring to the organization.

However, this tribunal does not find agreement in the demand of the workmen by raising 10% increment on gross salary who have completed 21 years of service, 15%
increment on gross salary who have completed 11 to 20 years of service, 10% increment on gross salary who have completed 1 to 10 years of service with the management.

The principles of equity and fairness would meet if the workmen are granted an annual 10%
increment in their overall salary from the date of reference i.e.
29.09.2016.
It aligns with the objective of providing reasonable appreciation for their loyalty, dedication, and expertise.
The said 10% annual increment serves as a means to bridge the wage disparity and acknowledge the skills and experience accumulated by the workmen over the years.
Additionally, the decision of this Tribunal is rooted in the jurisprudential concept of "human capital".
Human capital refers to the skills, knowledge, and experience possessed by employees, which significantly contribute to an organization's success and growth.

By rewarding the knowledge and experience of the workmen through an annual increment, the management of Chelmsford Club would be making a prudent investment in its human capital, fostering expertise that is integral to its future innovation and prosperity.

24. Keeping in view the reasoning aforesaid, this tribunal holds the workmen herein are entitled to an annual increment of 10% of their overall salary from the date of reference i.e.

The second point of concern pertains to various allowances demanded by the workmen of the Chelmsford Club,
encompassing House Rent Allowance (H.R.A.), food allowance,
conveyance allowance, washing allowance, and education allowance for their children, wherein the workman has sought 30%
House Rent Allowance on gross salary, food allowance of Rs.
1500/- per month, conveyance allowance of Rs. 3000/- per month ,
and washing allowance of Rs. 200/- per month and Rs. 1500/- as education allowances.
26.

With regards to the demand for House Rent Allowance (H.R.A.) at 30% of the gross salary, the Tribunal acknowledges the compelling circumstances of the high cost of living and housing in the city of Delhi.
The payment qua HRA is already being given to the workmen and thus is not a new demand but only amount is sought to be raised.
The Tribunal recognizes the principles of social justice and human dignity, which necessitate the provision of adequate housing for the workmen.

Considering the escalating property prices and rental rates, the H.R.A. request finds justification as it enables the workmen to meet their residential needs and maintain a respectable standard of living for themselves ID No. 9271/16 Page No. 20 of 32  and their families.
27.
Already the management as per the salary slip is giving a meager amount of Rs. 285/- which is sought to be raised.
The demand for food allowance of Rs. 1500/- per month is also deemed reasonable and essential.
The Tribunal recognizes that proper nutrition is fundamental to the well-being and productivity of the workmen.

In urban settings like Delhi, where the cost of living is significantly higher, this allowance is an apt measure to assist the workmen in meeting their dietary requirements, ensuring their overall health and work efficiency.

"61. We would now examine the process by which an Industrial Tribunal comes to its decisions and I have no hesitation in holding that the process employed is not judicial process at all.
In settling the disputes between the employers and the workmen, the function of the Tribunal is not confined to administration of justice in accordance with law.
It can confer rights and privileges on either party which it considers reasonable and proper, though they may not be within the terms of any existing agreement.
It has not merely to interpret or give effect to the contractual rights and obligations of the parties.
It can create new rights and obligations between them which it considers essential for keeping industrial peace.."

It is well settled that industrial adjudication under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 14 of 1947 is given wide powers and jurisdiction to make appropriate awards in determining industrial disputes brought before it.

An award made in an industrial adjudication may impose new obligations on the employer in the interest of social justice and with a view to secure peace and harmony between the employer and his workmen and full co-operation between them.
